title: Predictors that move together
objectives: Recognise collinearity and its effect on coefficients and their errors.

screens.title: Two months, two stories
screens.prose: A desk regresses next-hour returns (bp) on two signals, A and B. Both measure order-book imbalance, so they move almost together. The model was fitted on two separate months.

state.caption: Same model, two months of 20 days. Signals A and B have correlation 0.98.

screens.question: Which quantity did the two months agree on?

options.text: $\hat\beta_A + \hat\beta_B$
$\hat\beta_A$
options.why: Month 1 says 1.392 and month 2 says $-0.482$: not even the same sign.

options.text: $\hat\beta_B$
options.why: $\hat\beta_B$ moves from $-0.335$ to 1.560, a swing of nearly 1.9.

options.text: $\hat\beta_A - \hat\beta_B$
options.why: That is 1.727 in month 1 and $-2.042$ in month 2. Try adding instead.

hints.text: Both $R^2$ values are close. Look for a combination of the two coefficients that is close too.
Add the two coefficients in each row.

feedback.correct: The sum is 1.057 in month 1 and 1.078 in month 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Combine the two coefficients in each row, then compare the months.

byKey.a: You compared $\hat\beta_A$ across months. It flips sign, so it is the least stable number here.

explain.text: Each coefficient swings and even flips sign, yet the sum stays near 1.06 and $R^2$ near 0.78. When A and B move together, the data show what one unit of both does, not how to split it. That is **collinearity**.

screens.title: Squeezing the predictors together
screens.prose: The ellipse holds the plausible pairs $(\beta_A, \beta_B)$ from a fit of 100 days, true values $(0.5, 0.5)$. The slider sets the correlation $r$ between the two signals. Everything else stays the same.

derive.caption: SE of $\hat\beta_A$: {{fixed(0.1/sqrt(1 - r*r), 3)}}, which is {{fixed(1/sqrt(1 - r*r), 2)}} times its value at $r = 0$

screens.question: Set $r = 0.95$. How many times larger is the standard error of $\hat\beta_A$ than at $r = 0$?

hints.text: Drag the slider to 0.95 and read the caption.
The caption gives the factor directly. Watch the ellipse as you go.

feedback.correct: At $r = 0.95$ the standard error is 3.2 times as large.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the slider to 0.95 and read the factor in the caption.

byKey.variance: That is the factor on the variance, $1/(1 - r^2)$. The standard error is its square root.
byKey.r: That is the correlation itself. Read the factor from the caption at $r = 0.95$.

explain.text: As $r$ rises the ellipse stretches along the dashed line $\beta_A + \beta_B = 1$. Across that line it stays thin: the sum is pinned. Along it, the split between A and B becomes almost anything.

screens.title: The variance inflation factor
screens.prose: You found the standard error 3.20 times larger at $r = 0.95$. The **variance** grows by the square of that factor. We call that square the **variance inflation factor**, VIF.
screens.question: What is the VIF at $r = 0.95$?

hints.text: Square the factor 3.20.
Or compute $1/(1 - r^2)$ directly.

feedback.correct: A VIF of 10.26: the variance is ten times what it would be with uncorrelated signals.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The VIF is $1/(1 - r^2)$, the square of the standard error factor.

byKey.se: That is the standard error factor. The VIF is its square.
byKey.no-square: You used $1/(1 - r)$. The formula squares the correlation: $1/(1 - r^2)$.

explain.text: $\mathrm{VIF} = 1/(1 - 0.95^2) = 10.26$. A VIF above 10 is the usual warning sign. It means the data carry as much information about $\beta_A$ as about a tenth as many days.

screens.title: Why $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is the culprit
screens.prose: Centre both signals and scale them to variance 1. Then $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} = n\begin{bmatrix} 1 & r \\ r & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ for the slopes, and $\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}$.
screens.question: At $r = 0.99$, what is the top-left entry of the inverse?

hints.text: The top-left entry is $\tfrac{1}{1 - r^2} \times 1$.

feedback.correct: 50.25: the variance of $\hat\beta_A$ is 50 times its uncorrelated value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\tfrac{1}{1 - r^2}$ at $r = 0.99$.

byKey.no-sq: You used $1/(1 - r)$. The determinant is $1 - r^2$.
byKey.det: That is the determinant, $1 - r^2$. The entry is its reciprocal.

explain.text: The determinant $1 - r^2 = 0.0199$ is nearly 0, so the inverse is huge: 50.25 on the diagonal. The off-diagonal $-r/(1 - r^2)$ is just as large and negative. That negative covariance is why one coefficient rises when the other falls.

screens.title: The condition number
screens.prose: The eigenvalues of $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & r \\ r & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ are $1 + r$, along $(1, 1)$, and $1 - r$, along $(1, -1)$. The **condition number** is the largest over the smallest. The eigenvalues course used it to measure how close a matrix is to singular.
screens.question: What is the condition number at $r = 0.95$?

hints.text: Divide the larger eigenvalue by the smaller.
The eigenvalues are 1.95 and 0.05.

feedback.correct: 39: the matrix is 39 times stiffer in one direction than the other.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $1 + r$ by $1 - r$.

byKey.vif: That is the VIF. The condition number compares the two eigenvalues.
byKey.inv: You divided the small eigenvalue by the large one. Put the larger on top.

explain.text: The data spread widely along $(1, 1)$, so the sum $\beta_A + \beta_B$ is well measured. Along $(1, -1)$ the eigenvalue is 0.05: almost no days separate A from B. That thin direction is the long axis of the ellipse.

screens.title: When one signal is a copy
screens.prose: A data error stores signal B as exactly $2 \times$ signal A. Now $r = 1$, and the columns of $\mathbf{X}$ are dependent.
screens.question: What does least squares give for $\beta_A$ and $\beta_B$?

options.text: No single answer: every pair with the same $\beta_A + 2\beta_B$ fits equally well
One answer, with very large standard errors
options.why: That is near collinearity. With an exact copy $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is singular and has no inverse at all.

options.text: $\beta_B = 0$, since B adds nothing new
options.why: Some software drops a column for you. The equations themselves allow a whole line of answers.

options.text: $\beta_A = \beta_B$, splitting the effect evenly
options.why: Nothing in the data prefers an even split. Any pair on the line fits the same.

hints.text: Column B is twice column A. What does that do to $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta$?
$\beta_A A + \beta_B B = (\beta_A + 2\beta_B) A$.
Only $\beta_A + 2\beta_B$ affects the fit, so $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is singular and the solution is a line.

feedback.correct: Only $\beta_A + 2\beta_B$ is identified; the split is not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\beta_A A + \beta_B B$ using $B = 2A$.

byKey.huge: You treated exact collinearity like near collinearity. Here $\det(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}) = 0$, so there is no inverse.
byKey.zero: You let the software choose. Mathematically $\beta_B = 0$ is just one point on the line of solutions.

explain.text: Row 3 of $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is twice row 2, so its determinant is 0. Every pair with the same $\beta_A + 2\beta_B$ fits identically, and NumPy's `solve` may raise an error. Worse, rounding can leave a tiny nonzero determinant; then it silently returns one arbitrary point on that line.

screens.title: Two weak signals?
screens.prose: Next-month stock returns (%) on 6-month and 12-month momentum, over 120 months. The signals have correlation 0.95. A colleague says: neither $t$ clears 1.96, so drop both.
screens.question: What do these numbers support?

options.text: Together they predict returns; the data cannot split the credit
Neither signal matters, so drop both
options.why: You read each small $t$ as no effect. The $F$ test asks about both at once: $p = 0.0004$.

options.text: Keep mom6 and drop mom12, the weaker one
options.why: You chose by $t$, but with $r = 0.95$ either one alone looks strong. Alone, mom12 has $t = 3.68$.

options.text: Long 12-month momentum loses money: its coefficient is negative
options.why: You read the sign swing as a real effect. Alone, mom12 has slope $+0.505$ and $t = 3.68$.

hints.text: Which line tests both signals together?
The $F$-statistic asks whether both slopes are zero at once.
$F = 8.3$ with $p = 0.0004$: together they matter. The large standard errors come from $r = 0.95$, a VIF of 10.3.

feedback.correct: The joint test is strong; the individual $t$ values are small because the signals share their information.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the individual $t$ values with the joint $F$ test.

byKey.drop: You read each small $t$ as no effect. Collinearity inflated both standard errors by $\sqrt{10.3} = 3.2$; the $F$ test is clear.
byKey.neg: You read a collinear coefficient's sign as real. Fitted alone, mom12 has slope $+0.505$ and $t = 3.68$.

explain.text: Alone, mom6 has $t = 4.06$ and mom12 has $t = 3.68$. Together their VIF is 10.3, so each standard error is 3.2 times larger and each $t$ shrinks. The $F$ test, with $p = 0.0004$, says the pair matters.

screens.title: Deriving the VIF
screens.prose: Why is the factor $1/(1 - r^2)$? Centre both predictors and scale them to variance 1, so the intercept separates out. Put the steps in order.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}$, the covariance of least squares coefficients
$\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} = n\begin{bmatrix} 1 & r \\ r & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, since each scaled column has $\sum x^2 = n$ and $\sum x_A x_B = nr$
At $r = 0$ this is $\sigma^2/n$, so the inflation factor is $1/(1 - r^2)$

hints.text: Start from the general covariance formula.
Build $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ before inverting it.
Formula, then the matrix, then its inverse, then read off the entry, then compare with $r = 0$.

feedback.correct: The factor comes from the determinant $1 - r^2$ of the correlation matrix.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ before you can invert it.

byKey.inv: You inverted before building the matrix. Write $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ first.
byKey.ratio: The comparison with $r = 0$ comes last, once $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_A)$ is written down.

explain.text: With more predictors the same steps give $\mathrm{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)$. Here $R_j^2$ is the $R^2$ from regressing $x_j$ on all the other predictors. With two predictors, $R_j^2 = r^2$.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: For predictor $j$, regress $x_j$ on all the other predictors and call that fit's $R^2$ $R_j^2$. Then $$\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_j) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\textstyle\sum (x_{ij} - \bar x_j)^2}}\sqrt{\mathrm{VIF}_j}, \qquad \mathrm{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}.$$ The fitted values and $R^2$ are unaffected; only the split between predictors is.
screens.question: Regressing $x_3$ on $x_1$ and $x_2$ gives $R^2 = 0.90$. What is $\mathrm{VIF}_3$?

options.why: You computed $1/R_j^2$. The VIF is $1/(1 - R_j^2)$.
That is $\sqrt{10}$, the factor on the standard error, not the variance.
That is $R_j^2$ itself.

explain.text: $\mathrm{VIF}_3 = 1/0.10 = 10$. So the standard error of $\hat\beta_3$ is $\sqrt{10} = 3.16$ times what it would be with $x_3$ unrelated to the others.

screens.title: What to do about it
screens.prose: Back to mom6 and mom12, with correlation 0.95 and VIF 10.3. You want a model you can trade and explain.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which are sound responses?

options.text: Keep one signal and drop the other
Combine them into one signal, such as their average
Replace them with their first principal component
Keep both, but report only the combined effect
Keep the one with the larger $t$ in the joint fit and call the other useless
options.why: You judged by the joint $t$. Alone, mom12 has $t = 3.68$; it is not useless, just redundant.

options.text: Add a third momentum signal to break the tie
options.why: You added more of the same. A third correlated signal raises every VIF further.

hints.text: A remedy either removes the overlap or stops asking the data to split it.
Principal components come from the eigenvectors of the correlation matrix; the first is the $(1, 1)$ direction.
Four are sound: drop one, average them, use the first principal component, or report only the sum.

feedback.correct: All four sound remedies either remove the overlap or stop asking for the split.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask of each option: does it remove the overlap, or still ask the data to split the credit?

byKey.t: You judged by $t$ inside the collinear fit. That $t$ is shrunk by the overlap, not by weakness.
byKey.more: You added another correlated signal. That makes $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ closer to singular, not further.

explain.text: Dropping one or averaging both gives $t$ near 4 and almost the same $R^2$. The first principal component is the $(1, 1)$ eigenvector, which is the average up to scale. Reporting only the sum accepts that only the sum is identified.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def vifs(cols):
    X = np.column_stack(cols).astype(float)
    n, p = X.shape
    out = []
    for j in range(p):
        target = X[:, j]
        others = np.delete(X, j, axis=1)
        A = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), others])
        coef = np.linalg.lstsq(A, target, rcond=None)[0]
        resid = target - A @ coef
        dev = target - target.mean()
        r2 = 1 - (resid @ resid) / (dev @ dev)
        out.append(1 / (1 - r2))
    return out

examples.call: [round(float(v), 4) for v in vifs([mom6, mom12, size])]

tests.call: [round(float(v), 4) for v in vifs([mom6, mom12, size])]

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests. Each list of VIFs is rounded to 4 places and compared with `math.isclose`; the expected values match statsmodels' `variance_inflation_factor`. The first run loads NumPy, which takes several seconds.

hints.text: The residual is the target minus its fitted values, `A @ coef`.
$R_j^2 = 1 - \mathrm{SSE}/\mathrm{SST}$, with `resid @ resid` and `dev @ dev`.
`resid = target - A @ coef`, `r2 = 1 - (resid @ resid) / (dev @ dev)`, `out.append(1 / (1 - r2))`.

feedback.correct: For the ten stocks the VIFs are about 34.9, 36.4 and 1.40.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Two uncorrelated columns, such as `[1, -1, 1, -1]` and `[1, 1, -1, -1]`, must give `[1.0, 1.0]`.

byKey.test-1: For the ten stocks the answer is about `[34.9197, 36.3583, 1.3979]`. Check that the residual uses `A @ coef`.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace each `...` with an expression.

explain.text: Running `vifs([mom6, mom12, size])` gives about 34.9 and 36.4 for the momentum pair and 1.40 for size. Market cap and its log give VIFs near 4.7: the same information twice. Keep one of each pair before the backtest.

ideas: When predictors move together, the data pin down their combined effect but not the split, so single coefficients swing and their standard errors balloon.
$\mathrm{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)$ measures the damage; correlations and the condition number of the correlation matrix diagnose it. Fitted values and $R^2$ are unaffected.
Remedies: drop one, combine them, use principal components, or report only the sum. An exact copy makes $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ singular.

formula.name: Variance inflation factor
formula.note: With two predictors $R_j^2 = r^2$; a VIF above 10 is the usual alarm.

summary.trap: A small $t$ on a collinear predictor does not mean it is useless. A sign that flips is not a real effect either. Check the joint $F$ test and the VIFs first.

quiz.question: By what factor is the standard error of each slope inflated, compared with uncorrelated predictors?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The standard error factor is $\sqrt{\mathrm{VIF}} = 1/\sqrt{1 - r^2}$.

byKey.vif: That is the VIF, the factor on the variance. Take its square root.
byKey.no-sq: You used $1/(1 - r)$. Square the correlation first.

explain.text: $\mathrm{VIF} = 1/(1 - 0.64) = 2.78$, so the standard error grows by $\sqrt{2.78} = 1.67$. Correlation 0.8 sounds high but costs much less than 0.95.

quiz.prose: A model of stock returns includes both size (log market cap) and market cap in £bn. Each slope has $|t| < 1$, the $F$ test has $p = 0.001$, and the VIFs are both near 9.
quiz.question: What is the best reading?

options.text: The two predictors carry the same information; together they matter
Size has no effect on returns
options.why: You read each small $t$ alone. The $F$ test says the pair matters.

options.text: The $R^2$ is unreliable because of collinearity
options.why: Collinearity leaves $R^2$ and the fitted values unchanged; only the split is unstable.

options.text: Both coefficients are biased
options.why: Collinearity makes the estimates noisy, not biased: their average over samples is still right.

feedback.correct: Same information twice: keep one of them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the joint test and the VIFs together.

explain.text: Log market cap and market cap rank stocks almost identically, so VIFs near 9 are expected. The $F$ test shows size matters; the data just cannot split the credit. Keep one measure.

quiz.prose: A dataset has columns for a stock's return in % and the same return as a decimal. Both go into one regression with an intercept.
quiz.question: What happens to $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$?

options.text: It is singular: one column is 100 times the other
It is invertible, with large standard errors
options.why: That is near collinearity. An exact multiple makes the determinant exactly 0.

options.text: Nothing: the units differ, so the columns differ
options.why: Different units are just a rescaling. The columns are still exact multiples.

options.text: It is singular only if there is no intercept
options.why: The problem is between the two return columns, with or without the ones.

feedback.correct: Exact multiples make the columns dependent and $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ singular.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two return columns.

explain.text: The % column is 100 times the decimal column, so $\mathbf{X}$ has dependent columns and $\det(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}) = 0$. Only $100\beta_{\%}$ plus $\beta_{\text{dec}}$ is identified.

quiz.question: What is the condition number of their correlation matrix?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The eigenvalues are $1 + r$ and $1 - r$.

byKey.vif: That is the VIF, $1/(1 - r^2)$. The condition number divides the eigenvalues.
byKey.inv: You put the small eigenvalue on top.

explain.text: The eigenvalues are 1.9 and 0.1, so the condition number is 19. It grows without bound as $r \to 1$.
